new.q: [Circuits | Capacitance | Tier 3] A 20 kΩ resistor charges a 50 µF capacitor from a battery. What is the time constant τ = RC? (seconds)
new.w: Forgetting the µ (10⁻⁶) makes the answer a million times too large.
sol: Time constant is a product, not a sum.

new.q: [Circuits | Capacitance | Tier 7] A capacitor charges through a resistor from a 12 V supply. How many volts is it at after 2 time constants?
new.w: After one τ the capacitor is at 63%, not 100%, and never exactly reaches the supply.
sol: The curve rises fast at first then flattens.
Use v = Vs(1 − e^(−t/τ)) with t/τ = 2.
v = 12(1 − e^−2) = 10.4 V. Trap: After one τ the capacitor is at 63%, not 100%, and never exactly reaches the supply.

new.q: [Circuits | Capacitance | Tier 9] With τ = 1 s, a capacitor charges from 0 V toward a 10 V supply. How many seconds until it reaches 8 V?
new.w: Using ln(V/Vs) instead of ln(1 − V/Vs) gives a negative time: the curve tracks the REMAINING gap.
sol: Rearrange the charging equation to solve for time (a logarithm).
t = −τ ln(1 − V/Vs).
t = −1 ln(1 − 8/10) = 1.61 s. Trap: Using ln(V/Vs) instead of ln(1 − V/Vs) gives a negative time: the curve tracks the REMAINING gap.

new.q: [Circuits | Capacitance | Tier 11] A 250 µF capacitor discharges through a relay coil of 400 Ω. The relay stays closed while the capacitor is above 2 V; it starts at 8 V. How long (in ms) does the relay hold?

new.q: [Circuits | Capacitance | Tier 5] A 100 µF and a 300 µF capacitor are connected in series. What is the equivalent capacitance (µF)?
new.w: Using the resistor rules for capacitors swaps the two answers.
sol: Capacitors are the opposite of resistors for series and parallel.
Parallel adds. Series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂.
C = C₁C₂/(C₁+C₂) = 75 µF. Trap: Using the resistor rules for capacitors swaps the two answers.

new.q: [Circuits | Capacitance | Tier 9] A 10 V supply charges a capacitor through 10 kΩ with τ = 1 s. What is the charging current (in mA) at t = 2 s?

I = (10/10 000)e^−2 = 0.135 mA. Trap: The starting current Vs/R = 1 mA is NOT the answer at 2 s; it has already fallen.

new.q: [Circuits | DC circuits | Tier 9] A divider has R₁ = 1 kΩ on top and R₂ = 1 kΩ on the bottom across 12 V. A 1 kΩ load is connected across R₂. What is the load voltage?
new.w: The unloaded divider answer ignores that the load drags the voltage down.
sol: The load changes the bottom resistance.
Replace R₂ and the load by their parallel equivalent, then divide.
R₂‖R_L = 0.5 kΩ, so V = 12×0.5/(1+0.5) = 4 V. Trap: The unloaded divider answer ignores that the load drags the voltage down.

new.q: [Circuits | DC circuits | Tier 12] A 12 V source has 4 Ω of internal resistance. What is the largest power (in watts) it can deliver to a load resistor?
new.w: Using the whole V²/R_s (4× too high) forgets that half the voltage is lost inside the source.
sol: Delivered power rises, peaks, then falls as the load changes.
The peak is when the load equals the internal resistance.
R_L = 4 Ω, current = 12/8 A, P = I²R = 9 W. Trap: Using the whole V²/R_s (4× too high) forgets that half the voltage is lost inside the source.

new.q: [Circuits | V, I, R, P, E | Tier 7] A battery has EMF 12 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω. What is its terminal voltage while supplying 4 A?
new.w: Adding I·r instead of subtracting it gives a terminal voltage above the EMF, which is impossible while discharging.
sol: Some voltage is lost inside the battery itself.
Terminal voltage = EMF − I·r.
V = 12 − 4×0.5 = 10 V. Trap: Adding I·r instead of subtracting it gives a terminal voltage above the EMF, which is impossible while discharging.

new.q: [Circuits | Kirchhoff | Tier 8] A Wheatstone bridge is balanced with R₁ = 100 Ω and R₂ = 200 Ω in one arm pair and R₃ = 150 Ω with R₄ unknown (R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄). Find R₄ in ohms.
new.w: Inverting one ratio gives R₄ = R₁R₃/R₂, which is wrong.
sol: At balance no current flows through the meter.
Set the two ratios equal and solve for R₄.
R₄ = R₂R₃/R₁ = 200×150/100 = 300 Ω. Trap: Inverting one ratio gives R₄ = R₁R₃/R₂, which is wrong.

new.q: [Circuits | DC circuits | Tier 7] 3 A enters a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 3 Ω resistors. How many amps flow through the 6 Ω resistor?
new.w: Using its own resistance in the numerator gives the other branch’s current.
sol: Current prefers the easier path.
Current in one branch = total × (the OTHER resistance) / (sum).
I = 3×3/(6+3) = 1 A. Trap: Using its own resistance in the numerator gives the other branch’s current.

new.q: [Circuits | DC circuits | Tier 12] A 12 V source feeds a divider R₁ = 3 kΩ, R₂ = 6 kΩ. What is the Thevenin resistance (Ω) seen by a load across R₂?
new.w: Adding R₁ + R₂ is the series mistake; the shorted source ties R₁ to the other rail.
sol: Short the source and look back into the output terminals.
With the source shorted, R₁ and R₂ are in parallel.
R_th = R₁‖R₂ = 2e+03 Ω. Trap: Adding R₁ + R₂ is the series mistake; the shorted source ties R₁ to the other rail.

new.q: [Circuits | Diodes & LEDs | Tier 7] An LED with a 2 V forward drop must carry 20 mA from a 9 V supply. What series resistor (Ω) is needed?
new.w: Using the full supply voltage gives a resistor that is too big and a dim LED.
sol: The resistor only sees the voltage the LED does not use.
R = (Vs − Vf)/I.
R = (9 − 2)/0.02 = 350 Ω. Trap: Using the full supply voltage gives a resistor that is too big and a dim LED.

new.q: [Circuits | Diodes & LEDs | Tier 7] An LED with a 2 V forward drop must carry 10 mA from a 5 V supply. What series resistor (Ω) is needed?
new.w: Using the full supply voltage gives a resistor that is too big and a dim LED.
sol: The resistor only sees the voltage the LED does not use.
R = (Vs − Vf)/I.
R = (5 − 2)/0.01 = 300 Ω. Trap: Using the full supply voltage gives a resistor that is too big and a dim LED.

new.q: [Circuits | Diodes & LEDs | Tier 7] An LED with a 3 V forward drop must carry 20 mA from a 12 V supply. What series resistor (Ω) is needed?
new.w: Using the full supply voltage gives a resistor that is too big and a dim LED.
sol: The resistor only sees the voltage the LED does not use.
R = (Vs − Vf)/I.
R = (12 − 3)/0.02 = 450 Ω. Trap: Using the full supply voltage gives a resistor that is too big and a dim LED.

new.q: [Circuits | Diodes & LEDs | Tier 7] An LED with a 2 V forward drop must carry 16 mA from a 6 V supply. What series resistor (Ω) is needed?
new.w: Using the full supply voltage gives a resistor that is too big and a dim LED.
sol: The resistor only sees the voltage the LED does not use.
R = (Vs − Vf)/I.
R = (6 − 2)/0.016 = 250 Ω. Trap: Using the full supply voltage gives a resistor that is too big and a dim LED.

new.q: [Circuits | Magnetism & induction | Tier 3] A relay coil has 400 Ω resistance and pulls in at 8 V. What coil current (mA) flows at pull-in?
new.w: Mixing up volts and amps leads to answers near 50 instead of 20.
sol: The coil is just a resistor for steady DC.
I = V/R.
I = 8/400 = 20 mA. Trap: Mixing up volts and amps leads to answers near 50 instead of 20.

new.q: [Circuits | Magnetism & induction | Tier 3] A relay coil has 385 Ω resistance and pulls in at 7.67 V. What coil current (mA) flows at pull-in?
new.w: Mixing up volts and amps leads to answers near 50 instead of 20.
sol: The coil is just a resistor for steady DC.
I = V/R.
I = 7.67/385 = 19.9 mA. Trap: Mixing up volts and amps leads to answers near 50 instead of 20.

new.q: [Circuits | Magnetism & induction | Tier 5] What is the time constant (ms) of a 0.5 H inductor in series with 100 Ω?
new.w: Using R·L (the RC form) is the rule-confusion trap.
sol: Inductive time constants divide, capacitive ones multiply.
τ = L/R.
τ = 0.5/100 = 5 ms. Trap: Using R·L (the RC form) is the rule-confusion trap.

new.q: [Circuits | Magnetism & induction | Tier 5] What is the time constant (ms) of a 2 H inductor in series with 400 Ω?
new.w: Using R·L (the RC form) is the rule-confusion trap.
sol: Inductive time constants divide, capacitive ones multiply.
τ = L/R.
τ = 2/400 = 5 ms. Trap: Using R·L (the RC form) is the rule-confusion trap.

new.q: [Circuits | DC & AC | Tier 4] A sine wave peaks at 170 V. What is its RMS voltage?
new.w: Multiplying by √2 (instead of dividing) goes the wrong way.
sol: RMS is the DC value that gives the same heating.
Vrms = Vpeak/√2.
170/1.414 = 120 V. Trap: Multiplying by √2 (instead of dividing) goes the wrong way.

new.q: [Circuits | DC & AC | Tier 4] A sine wave peaks at 10 V. What is its RMS voltage?
new.w: Multiplying by √2 (instead of dividing) goes the wrong way.
sol: RMS is the DC value that gives the same heating.
Vrms = Vpeak/√2.
10/1.414 = 7.07 V. Trap: Multiplying by √2 (instead of dividing) goes the wrong way.

new.q: [Circuits | DC & AC | Tier 4] A sine wave peaks at 325 V. What is its RMS voltage?
new.w: Multiplying by √2 (instead of dividing) goes the wrong way.
sol: RMS is the DC value that gives the same heating.
Vrms = Vpeak/√2.
325/1.414 = 230 V. Trap: Multiplying by √2 (instead of dividing) goes the wrong way.

new.q: [Circuits | Capacitance | Tier 7] A hovercraft timer charges a capacitor through a resistor. You double the resistor, keeping the supply and capacitor. What changes?
o: It takes twice as long to reach any given voltage
It reaches twice the final voltage
It stores twice the energy at full charge
It charges to the same voltage in half the time
new.w: Mixing speed with final value: R sets how fast, not how much.
sol: Think about what limits the current.
τ = RC, so doubling R doubles τ.
A bigger R only slows the charging; the final voltage is still the supply. Trap: Mixing speed with final value: R sets how fast, not how much.

new.q: [Circuits | Capacitance | Tier 9] On a relay-hold timer the capacitor discharges through the coil. Which change makes the relay stay closed LONGER?
o: A larger capacitor
A coil with lower resistance
A lower starting voltage
A higher drop-out voltage
new.w: Lower coil resistance feels like “easier flow” but it empties the capacitor faster.
sol: Longer hold means more time before the voltage falls to the drop-out level.
t = RC ln(V₀/V₁).
Larger C increases RC. Lower R, lower V₀ or higher V₁ all shorten the hold. Trap: Lower coil resistance feels like “easier flow” but it empties the capacitor faster.

new.q: [Circuits | Capacitance | Tier 5] After about how many time constants is a charging capacitor within 1% of its final voltage?
new.w: After 1τ the capacitor is at 63%, which many students remember as “charged”.
sol: Each τ closes about 63% of the remaining gap.
After 5τ the remaining gap is 0.7%. Trap: After 1τ the capacitor is at 63%, which many students remember as “charged”.

new.q: [Circuits | Capacitance | Tier 9] Two capacitors of different sizes are connected in series to a battery. Which statement is true?
o: Same charge on each; the smaller capacitor has the larger voltage
Same voltage on each; the smaller capacitor holds less charge
Same charge on each; the larger capacitor has the larger voltage
Different charges on each; the voltages are equal
new.w: Copying the resistor rule “bigger gets more voltage” reverses the result.
sol: What is the same for every component in a series chain?
Q = CV and Q is the same, so V is bigger where C is smaller.
The series chain passes equal charge; the voltage splits inversely to capacitance. Trap: Copying the resistor rule “bigger gets more voltage” reverses the result.

new.q: [Circuits | DC circuits | Tier 5] A third resistor is added in PARALLEL with two resistors already connected to a battery. What happens to the total resistance and the battery current?
o: Resistance falls and battery current rises
Resistance rises and current falls
Resistance and current both stay the same
Resistance falls and current falls
new.w: Adding a component does not automatically add resistance; that is only for series.
sol: Every extra parallel path is another route for current.
Total conductance adds, so total R decreases.
Smaller R with the same voltage means bigger current. Trap: Adding a component does not automatically add resistance; that is only for series.

new.q: [Circuits | DC circuits | Tier 9] Two identical bulbs are in series with a battery. One bulb is shorted with a wire. What happens to the other bulb?
o: It gets brighter
It goes out
It stays the same
It gets dimmer
new.w: Assuming a short “kills” the circuit confuses a short across a part with a short across the source.
sol: Draw the circuit. What does the shorted bulb carry now?
The remaining bulb now sees the full battery voltage and a smaller total resistance.
Total resistance halves, current doubles, power in the working bulb is four times larger. Trap: Assuming a short “kills” the circuit confuses a short across a part with a short across the source.

new.q: [Circuits | V, I, R, P, E | Tier 6] The voltage across a fixed resistor is doubled. By what factor does its power change?
new.w: Treating power as proportional to voltage (V alone) misses the square.
sol: Power can be written with V and R only.
P = V²/R.
Doubling V squares to 4. Trap: Treating power as proportional to voltage (V alone) misses the square.

new.q: [Circuits | V, I, R, P, E | Tier 12] A source feeds a load. At the load value that gives MAXIMUM power, what is the efficiency?
new.w: “Maximum power” does not mean “maximum efficiency”; efficiency keeps rising with R_L.
sol: Compare the power in the load with the power in the internal resistance.
At the match R_L = R_s, they share the voltage equally and carry the same current.
Half the power is wasted inside the source. Trap: “Maximum power” does not mean “maximum efficiency”; efficiency keeps rising with R_L.

new.q: [Circuits | V, I, R, P, E | Tier 9] A battery’s terminal voltage drops when you draw more current. Why?
o: Voltage is lost across its internal resistance
The EMF itself falls as the current rises
The chemicals suddenly lose their stored energy
The connecting wires get longer at high current
new.w: Thinking the EMF itself changes confuses the ideal source with its real model.
sol: The battery is not a perfect source.
Model it as an ideal EMF with a small resistor in series.
V_terminal = EMF − I·r. Trap: Thinking the EMF itself changes confuses the ideal source with its real model.

new.q: [Circuits | Kirchhoff | Tier 8] A Wheatstone bridge is balanced. What is the reading of the meter across its middle?
o: Zero: the two midpoints sit at equal voltage
The full supply voltage appears across the meter
Half the supply voltage, whatever the resistors are
The average of the four resistor values, in volts
new.w: Confusing “balanced” with “all four resistors equal” – only the ratios must match.
sol: A balanced bridge is a statement about two voltage dividers.
Both dividers produce the same midpoint voltage.
Equal midpoint voltages mean no current in the meter. Trap: Confusing “balanced” with “all four resistors equal” – only the ratios must match.

new.q: [Circuits | DC circuits | Tier 10] A 10 MΩ voltmeter is placed across a 100 kΩ resistor in a divider. Another 10 MΩ meter is placed across a 10 MΩ resistor. Which reading is MORE distorted?
o: The one across the 10 MΩ resistor
The one across the 100 kΩ resistor
Both are the same
Neither; meters never change the circuit
new.w: Believing a voltmeter is perfect ignores loading.
sol: Compare the meter’s resistance with the part it measures.
Parallel combination changes the part a lot only when the two are similar.
10 MΩ ‖ 10 MΩ = 5 MΩ halves the resistance. Trap: Believing a voltmeter is perfect ignores loading.

new.q: [Circuits | Diodes & LEDs | Tier 9] A relay coil is driven by a transistor. Where does the flyback diode go and why?
o: Across the coil, reverse-biased, to carry the collapsing current
In series with the coil, forward-biased, to block reverse current
Across the battery, so that it cannot discharge by itself
From the transistor base to ground, to speed up switching
new.w: Putting the diode forward-biased in normal operation short-circuits the coil.
sol: What does an inductor do when the current is suddenly cut?
It tries to keep the current flowing, creating a large voltage spike.
The diode conducts only at turn-off and clamps the spike. Trap: Putting the diode forward-biased in normal operation short-circuits the coil.

new.q: [Circuits | Magnetism & induction | Tier 9] The relay current is switched off in 1 ms. Why does the transistor see a much larger voltage than the supply?
o: The coil’s collapsing field induces a voltage L·dI/dt
The battery voltage doubles when the switch opens
The capacitor dumps extra charge into the transistor
The resistor heats up and pushes charge back
new.w: Blaming the battery overlooks the inductor’s stored energy.
sol: A rapid change in current matters.
Faraday: induced voltage grows with how quickly the current falls.
A fast turn-off makes dI/dt large. Trap: Blaming the battery overlooks the inductor’s stored energy.

new.q: [Circuits | V, I, R, P, E | Tier 10] A hovercraft fan runs through long, thin wires and draws a large current. What happens to the voltage at the fan compared with the battery?
o: It is lower, by I × R of the wires
It is higher, because wires add voltage
It is identical, since wires have zero resistance
It oscillates
new.w: Treating wires as ideal ignores a voltage drop that matters at high current.
sol: Real wires have resistance.
Series wires drop I × R_wire.
A few ohms of wire at several amps cost volts and power. Trap: Treating wires as ideal ignores a voltage drop that matters at high current.

new.q: [Circuits | V, I, R, P, E | Tier 10] A fresh pack is labelled 12.0 V nominal but reads 12.6 V with no load, then 11.6 V when the fan runs. Which statement explains this?
o: Nominal is an average; real voltage depends on charge and load
The meter must be broken, since the label never changes
A battery always outputs exactly its labelled voltage
The fan adds voltage to the pack when it spins
new.w: “The label is the truth” is the nominal-versus-measured trap.
sol: Compare no-load with loaded readings.
Open-circuit voltage is higher than the loaded voltage because of internal resistance.
Always measure under the condition the rules or your design care about. Trap: “The label is the truth” is the nominal-versus-measured trap.

new.q: [Circuits | DC circuits | Tier 12] A motor spins up slowly. At the instant of switch-on, is the current larger or smaller than at full speed, and why?
o: Larger: the motor has no back-EMF until it speeds up
Smaller: the windings are still cold when it starts
The same: a battery always supplies constant current
Smaller: friction holds the motor back at the start
new.w: Assuming current must be steady forgets back-EMF.
sol: A spinning motor also acts like a generator.
Back-EMF opposes the supply and rises with speed.
At start, I = V/R_winding is large; at speed, I = (V − EMF)/R. Trap: Assuming current must be steady forgets back-EMF.

new.q: [Circuits | Digital logic | Tier 6] A 2-input NAND gate has inputs A = 1 and B = 1. What is the output, and what does the gate do to an input of 1 on both pins?
o: 0, because NAND is AND followed by NOT
1, because NAND is a version of the OR gate
1, because both of the inputs are high
0, because NAND is always switched off
new.w: Reading NAND as “not AND” means the opposite of AND’s truth table.
sol: Do AND first.
AND(1,1) = 1, then invert.
The output is 0, the only input pair that gives 0. Trap: Reading NAND as “not AND” means the opposite of AND’s truth table.
